notes.meaning: Nearby neighbors heard that the returned Jewish exiles had begun rebuilding the temple for the Lord in Jerusalem. These people were foreigners whom Assyrian kings had brought into the land long ago, and they mixed worship of the Lord with worship of their own idols. They asked to join the building project, but their real aim was to weaken the work and damage pure worship.

Zerubbabel and the other Jewish leaders rejected the offer right away. They explained that King Cyrus had ordered the Jewish people alone to rebuild the temple, and they could not partner with people who honored false gods. Idolatry—worshiping false gods—had sent their ancestors into exile in the first place, so they were determined to keep God's worship pure.

When their offer was refused, the neighboring people dropped their friendly mask and showed their true hostility. They tried to break the builders' courage and make them afraid to continue working. Their main goal was to discourage the people of Judah so they would drop their tools and quit.

The opponents went further by hiring advisers and lobbyists to work against the Jews at the Persian royal court. These paid agents spread rumors and created delays so building permits and supplies would be blocked. This steady pressure hindered the work throughout the rest of King Cyrus's reign and into the rule of King Darius.

Years later, when King Xerxes took power, the enemies sent a formal charge against the people of Jerusalem. The writer includes this fact to show that opposition never really stopped across many generations. Whenever God's people made progress, hostile neighbors tried to find ways to accuse them before the authorities.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Most modern scholars identify this ruler as Xerxes I and see verses 6 through 23 as a jump forward to later attacks against rebuilding the city walls, while many older commentators believed this was Cyrus's son Cambyses.

notes.meaning: During the reign of King Artaxerxes, another group of local officials wrote a letter to the Persian king against Jerusalem. The message was written in Aramaic, the common diplomatic language used across the Persian Empire. The enemies hoped the royal court would step in and crush Jewish efforts to rebuild.

Rehum the military commander and Shimshai the scribe drafted this official letter against the city of Jerusalem. Rehum held high civil and military authority in the province, while Shimshai was a royal secretary sent to keep official records. They used their political standing to turn the imperial government against the Jews.

The letter was signed on behalf of many different ethnic groups and officials across the province. These were peoples whom the Assyrian emperor Ashurbanipal had deported from places like Babylon, Persia, and Susa and settled in Samaria. Listing all these groups made it look like the entire region stood united against Jerusalem.

This verse gives the formal opening of the letter sent across the Euphrates River to King Artaxerxes. The writers presented themselves as humble, loyal servants living in the province west of the river. By using respectful court language, they sought to win the king's confidence before presenting their charges.

The officials warned the king that the Jews who had returned to Jerusalem were rebuilding the city and repairing its walls and foundations. They labeled Jerusalem a rebellious and wicked city, reminding the king of its ancient past. They falsely claimed that the Jews were preparing for war against Persia rather than just repairing their homes.

The letter warned that if Jerusalem's walls were finished, the Jews would stop paying tribute, tolls, and customs duties. These taxes included road fees, business charges, and annual payments to the Persian throne. The enemies knew that threatening the king's treasury was the fastest way to get his attention.

The accusers claimed they were speaking up only because they cared deeply about the king's honor and income. Their phrase about eating the salt of the palace meant they received their pay and support from the king. Underneath this show of royal devotion, they were really trying to protect their own local power.

The letter urged the king to check old imperial records to see that Jerusalem had rebelled against kings in past centuries. It noted that the city was destroyed originally because of this rebellious past. The accusers then exaggerated wildly, claiming that if the walls were rebuilt, the king would lose all control over the lands west of the Euphrates.

King Artaxerxes sent an official royal decree back to Rehum, Shimshai, and the other regional leaders in Samaria. The letter opened with the customary royal greeting wishing them peace. This reply gave the local officials the royal authority they wanted to use against the Jews.

The king stated that the letter sent to him had been translated and read aloud in his presence. Persian monarchs had officials translate Aramaic messages into the Persian language. The accusers' plan had succeeded, and their charges were now officially accepted by the king.

Artaxerxes reported that he had ordered a search of the royal chronicles, and the records confirmed Jerusalem's past revolts. Kings of Judah like Jehoiakim and Zedekiah had indeed rebelled against the Babylonian Empire in former times. The Persian king saw this historical record as a clear warning of possible future trouble.

The archives also showed that mighty kings had once ruled in Jerusalem over the whole region and gathered taxes from other nations. This looked back to powerful rulers like David and Solomon. Artaxerxes feared that if the city grew strong again, it might try to reclaim that same imperial power.

The king issued a command for the work in Jerusalem to stop immediately until he gave further orders. He acted on the one-sided report without checking whether the Jews actually planned any rebellion. Yet his words left open the possibility that a future decree might allow building to resume.

Artaxerxes gave strict orders to his officials not to delay in enforcing his ban. He wanted to make sure the royal treasury suffered no loss and the empire faced no growing rebellion. This command gave the Jewish enemies legal permission to shut down the rebuilding effort.

As soon as the king's letter arrived, Rehum, Shimshai, and their associates rushed to Jerusalem to stop the Jews by force. They brought soldiers and threats to compel the workers to drop their tools immediately. Their swift, forceful response proved that they were driven by deep hatred for the Jewish people.

The story now returns to the original temple project under Zerubbabel, which had been halted years earlier by enemy opposition. The construction of God's house stayed frozen until the second year of King Darius, a delay of about sixteen years. Although the work paused for a time, God was still preparing the way to finish His temple.
